title: Barbarossa Begins
subtitle: Surprise, resistance and the struggle to understand the opening day
author: R.G. Cruise
summary: The German assault shattered the frontier system unevenly. Its greatest immediate advantage was the ability to act coherently while Soviet headquarters struggled to discover what was happening.
body:
A war announced after it had begun

At 1 p.m. on 22 June 1941, the American embassy in Moscow reported that Vyacheslav Molotov had announced the German attack in a radio address beginning at 12:15. By then, the invasion had been under way for hours. The gap between the battlefield and the public announcement is an appropriate starting point for the first day: soldiers, airfield personnel and civilians in the western regions were already trying to survive a war that much of the country was only now being told had begun. Molotov, not Stalin, delivered the government’s first major broadcast. The surviving diplomatic report establishes the sequence without requiring an invented scene of what every listener thought or felt. [1] In Berlin the explanation had arrived earlier, but it was no less political. The American embassy reported that Joseph Goebbels read Hitler’s proclamation at 5:30 a.m., German summer time, announcing military action and invoking Finnish and Romanian participation. These were public accounts produced by governments seeking to define a war already in progress. They should be read alongside the months of German planning examined in Before the Storm, rather than accepted as evidence that the invasion had been improvised in response to a last-minute Soviet threat. [2] The military result of the day was immense but specific. Germany seized the initiative along a vast front, damaged Soviet aviation, penetrated frontier defences and disrupted the command systems on which an organized response depended. It did not destroy all Soviet military power or remove every obstacle from its path. Indeed, the coexistence of rapid penetration and determined local resistance was one of the day’s most consequential features. A formation could be fighting hard while the operational structure around it was collapsing; another could withdraw from a threatened position only to find German troops already beyond its intended destination. [3] This is why the first day is best understood as a contest over the ability to act. German headquarters generally knew what their forces were supposed to accomplish and had organized the opening accordingly. Soviet headquarters had to discover what was happening, locate their own formations, distinguish a local penetration from a major breakthrough and issue orders while their means of doing so were being attacked. The advantage was not an abstract superiority possessed equally by every German soldier. It was the practical benefit of an army already conducting its chosen operation against an opponent still trying to establish the terms of the battle.

The air offensive and the destruction of information

The Luftwaffe attacked Soviet airfields in the opening hours, seeking to destroy aircraft before they could intervene and to impair the bases from which surviving machines would operate. The blows were especially damaging in the western sectors, where forward deployments and incomplete dispersal exposed aircraft and supporting infrastructure. Runways and parked machines were only part of the target. Fuel, maintenance facilities, communications and the personnel who made sorties possible belonged to the same system. An aircraft that escaped destruction could still become unusable if it lost its base, supply arrangements or connection with the formations it was meant to support. [3] The familiar figure of approximately 1,200 Soviet aircraft lost on the first day requires attribution. Kipp presents it as a Soviet acknowledged total and identifies 758 losses with the Western Special Military District. Those figures are useful evidence of the scale and concentration of the disaster; they are not a reason to repeat every German victory claim or assume that the same accounting methods were used by both sides. The distinction between aircraft destroyed on the ground, lost in combat, abandoned or counted later matters. An exact-looking aggregate can conceal uncertainties in reporting that were themselves products of the attack. [4] The aerial offensive also attacked Soviet command indirectly. Aircraft observed roads and troop movements, bombed junctions and interfered with the passage of reserves. A headquarters deprived of air reconnaissance had less opportunity to determine where a German column was heading. A commander who received a report of tanks to his rear could not easily establish whether they belonged to a reconnaissance detachment, a substantial advance guard or the leading element of a larger formation. That uncertainty could encourage a premature withdrawal in one sector and a dangerously late one in another. The destruction of information magnified the destruction of equipment. Air superiority nevertheless had limits. Soviet aircraft continued to fly and Soviet forces continued to resist. The Luftwaffe’s ability to concentrate over selected routes did not mean that it possessed an uninterrupted view of every forest or road. Nor should the air losses be made to carry the entire explanation of the ground defeat. A division could lose contact with its army because telephone lines were cut, because the headquarters moved, because orders reached the wrong place or because the enemy had physically severed the route between them. Air power intensified these problems, but the invasion worked through the interaction of several arms. [5]

Counting losses

What “destroyed” can hide

An aircraft inventory, a combat claim and a formation’s return of serviceable machines answer different questions. The first-day figures in this study are attributed to the historical accounts that report them. They should not be read as a verified aircraft-by-aircraft register or added indiscriminately to losses reported for later days. [4]

Lithuania and the race for crossings

In the north, Wilhelm von Leeb’s Army Group North attacked from East Prussia into Lithuania. Erich Hoepner’s Fourth Panzer Group provided the principal mobile force, with Georg-Hans Reinhardt’s XLI Motorized Corps and Erich von Manstein’s LVI Motorized Corps operating on separate but related axes. Küchler’s Eighteenth Army and Busch’s Sixteenth Army followed and fought across a much broader frontage. Their opponent was Fyodor Kuznetsov’s Northwestern Front, formed from the Baltic Special Military District, with the Eighth and Eleventh Armies forward and the Twenty-seventh farther back. The German aim was to penetrate, disrupt those armies and gain the approaches to the Western Dvina before a coherent new defence could be established. [6] [3] The geography encouraged rapid movement along particular corridors rather than a uniform sweep. Rivers and bridges repeatedly narrowed the choices available to both attacker and defender. A crossing secured before demolition could allow a leading force to preserve momentum, while a destroyed bridge could require reconnaissance, engineers and a detour. Roads concentrated vehicles, making traffic discipline and the ordering of columns important. The first German successes created opportunities because Soviet forces had to respond to penetrations whose eventual direction was still uncertain. They did not abolish the physical constraints of the terrain. Hoth’s Third Panzer Group, although attacking through the southern part of Lithuania, belonged to Army Group Center. This command boundary is easy to miss on a broad campaign map. Its movement towards the Neman crossings was intended to open the northern arm of the operation against the Soviet forces in Belarus, not simply to reinforce Hoepner’s drive towards the Baltic. The approaches through Alytus and the Neman corridor therefore belonged to the central encirclement problem. Map proximity should not be allowed to replace the actual chain of command: neighbouring German columns could be pursuing different operational relationships. [6] For Kuznetsov’s command, the consequence was immediate pressure on both front-line divisions and the formations intended to strike back. The Third and Twelfth Mechanized Corps offered the means for a substantial counterattack, but they were not concentrated in one ready-made striking group. Their units had to move, establish contact and receive coherent tasks while the German advance and air attacks were changing the situation. The decisive tank battles around Raseiniai still lay ahead. On 22 June the important development was the creation of the conditions in which those counterattacks would be attempted: Soviet mobile reserves were being asked to restore a front already losing its shape. [4]

Brest and the two different meanings of resistance

Farther south, Guderian’s Second Panzer Group attacked across the Bug in the Brest sector, supported within Army Group Center’s operation by Kluge’s Fourth Army. Hoth’s northern movement and Guderian’s southern advance were designed to reach beyond the main Soviet concentration, while infantry armies pressed the front of the salient. The route through and around Brest mattered because it opened the southern approach towards the interior of Belarus. The fortress itself, however, became a battle whose duration and human experience did not match the speed of the mobile advance passing beyond it. [6] [7] Elements of Soviet units caught in the fortress organized resistance after the opening bombardment. The German formation directly associated with the assault was Fritz Schlieper’s Forty-fifth Infantry Division. The defence was carried on by groups that did not always share reliable communications or a single functioning command. Laila Akhmetova’s research into the participation of men from the 131st Light Artillery Regiment is a useful corrective to a purely emblematic account: the garrison included soldiers of different backgrounds and units whose individual experiences can disappear behind the later collective legend. The battle continued beyond the first day, even as the wider front moved east. [8] The operational distinction is essential. Holding out in a fortress could impose casualties, occupy an attacking formation and preserve resistance in a specific place. It did not necessarily stop the main panzer columns from using other routes. Conversely, the fact that those columns continued did not make the resistance meaningless to the men involved or to the Germans obliged to overcome it. These were different scales of effect. A history that turns the fortress into the obstacle that stopped the whole invasion exaggerates its operational role; one that treats it as irrelevant because the spearheads moved on misunderstands how a campaign accumulated costs. Dmitry Pavlov’s Western Front faced the same mismatch on a much larger scale. Its forward armies occupied a salient whose flanks were vulnerable to German penetration. The Third Army under Vasily Kuznetsov, the Tenth under Konstantin Golubev and the Fourth under Aleksandr Korobkov had to respond to attacks that threatened their communications with the rear as well as their front-line positions. The Thirteenth Army headquarters was still being brought into the developing arrangement. The main danger was not that every Soviet formation would be defeated in a frontal engagement. It was that formations still capable of fighting would be cut off from the roads and bridges on which their continued existence as organized armies depended. [3] [9] That danger was not fully visible from every headquarters on the first day. Reports arrived late or incompletely; commanders went forward to establish contact and became harder for their own staffs to reach. The German advance was exploiting a system in which damage to one connection could deprive several levels of command of reliable information. A unit might receive an order appropriate to the situation hours earlier and carry it out just as the enemy’s movement made it harmful. The resulting confusion was an operational condition with identifiable causes, not evidence that Soviet soldiers lacked the will to resist. [5]

Western Ukraine offers a different battle

Army Group South’s opening was less immediately decisive than the developments in the centre. Kleist’s First Panzer Group advanced with Reichenau’s Sixth Army on the northern part of Rundstedt’s front, while Stülpnagel’s Seventeenth Army attacked farther south. Their opponent, Kirponos’s Southwestern Front, possessed substantial forces and a command organization that retained more ability to respond than the rapidly dislocated headquarters farther north. Soviet resistance did not stop the invasion at the border, but it complicated the conversion of penetration into a large encirclement. The terrain and the distribution of forces would make the southern campaign follow its own pace. [5] The Soviet Fifth Army under Mikhail Potapov covered the northern approaches in this sector; Ivan Muzychenko’s Sixth Army operated farther south, with Fyodor Kostenko’s Twenty-sixth and Pavel Ponedelin’s Twelfth extending the front towards the Carpathians. Kleist’s penetration threatened the relationship between the Fifth and Sixth Armies and opened the routes towards Lutsk, Dubno and Rivne, known in many contemporary accounts as Rovno. These towns mattered as road and railway connections as well as destinations. A counterattack against the flank of a German column in this area could threaten the route supplying it even if the Soviet force did not recapture every village already passed. [6] [10] There was, however, a great distance between possessing mechanized corps and delivering a simultaneous blow with them. Some formations were near the threatened sector; others had to travel from deeper positions or change direction. A corps moving towards an assembly area could lose vehicles to breakdown, consume fuel intended for the battle and become separated from its artillery or infantry. An order to attack could therefore arrive when a commander had only part of the force listed against his name. These practical problems would dominate the following days, but their origins were already present on 22 June. The southern comparison is valuable because it prevents the collapse in Belarus from becoming a universal description of the entire Red Army. Kirponos’s headquarters could issue orders and organize resistance without possessing the means to make all of those orders succeed. German forces could gain ground while facing more sustained interference than their counterparts in the centre. Neither difference requires a claim that the Soviet southern counterattacks ultimately achieved their intended result. It means that the course of the campaign depended on where forces met, how they were organized and what opportunities their opponents could exploit. [5]

Names on the map

Rovno, Rivne and the same road junction

Contemporary German and Soviet records commonly use Rovno; the modern Ukrainian name is Rivne. Dvinsk and Dünaburg refer to Daugavpils, while the Western Dvina becomes the Daugava in Latvia. Recognizing these equivalents matters when following an operation across sources. A change of place name is not a change in the location of the battle. [6]

Moscow orders an offensive it cannot yet see

The central Soviet response developed through directives that became increasingly ambitious while the picture of the front remained incomplete. The second directive of 22 June ordered the destruction of enemy forces that had crossed the frontier and authorized air attacks into German territory. By evening, a third directive called for major counterstrokes. The Northwestern and Western Fronts were to converge towards Suwałki, while the Southwestern Front was to strike towards Lublin. The government was attempting to recover the initiative by imposing the offensive response anticipated in its planning on a situation already diverging sharply from that expectation. [3] These orders were not irrational simply because they called for counterattack. A penetrating enemy can be vulnerable at its flanks and along its supply routes. The problem was the scale and immediacy of the tasks relative to the Soviet formations’ actual condition. Headquarters could identify a desirable operational result without possessing the communications or concentration needed to achieve it. Orders directed towards distant objectives also risked keeping troops moving westward while German mobile forces were passing around them. In that setting, the relationship between the enemy’s speed and the age of one’s own information became lethal. Zhukov went to the Southwestern Front as a representative of the high command on the first day. His later account, considered in Ziemke and Bauer’s reconstruction, emphasized the need to establish the situation before attempting a concerted operation. The distinction between that practical concern and the expansive directives from Moscow exposes an important feature of the crisis. The Soviet command was not devoid of capable judgment. It lacked a system that consistently converted such judgment into feasible orders quickly enough, across formations already being disrupted. [5] The first day therefore ended with opposing expectations. German commanders were increasingly confident that the Soviet deployment could not respond coherently to the blow. Soviet leaders were ordering action intended to prove the opposite. In the following days, local counterattacks would sometimes inflict significant difficulty without reversing the operational situation. The distinction should be kept open at this point. On the evening of 22 June, the failure of every subsequent Soviet counterattack was not yet an accomplished fact, and German headquarters did not possess perfect knowledge of the reserves assembling against them. The orders also placed a heavy burden on the men who had to carry them out. A tank crew or infantry company might be told to advance without receiving a useful explanation of what had happened to the units beside it. For officers, the political danger of appearing passive could reinforce the military pressure to act. Yet moving immediately did not necessarily mean moving effectively. Some of the most costly Soviet actions of the opening period would arise from an effort to comply with a real strategic need—striking back—before the means for doing so had been brought together.

The first day for civilians and prisoners

For civilians in the frontier regions, the military distinctions translated into immediate practical questions: whether to remain at home, where roads led, whether transport existed and whether family members could be located. An official evacuation order, where issued, did not create enough vehicles or guarantee a safe route. Military columns, refugees and damaged infrastructure competed for space. The danger was not confined to people living exactly on the border. Air attacks and the movement of mobile forces could bring the war to a town before its inhabitants had received reliable information about the collapse farther west. The pattern of penetration recorded on the evening map helps explain why information and escape routes could become outdated together. [6] The populations affected did not share one relationship to Soviet rule. Some had experienced occupation, deportation, confiscation or imprisonment; others identified with the Soviet state or worked within its institutions. Jewish communities had particular reasons to fear German occupation, although knowledge of Nazi persecution did not always translate into knowledge of the killing policies about to unfold locally. No single photograph of a welcoming crowd, fleeing family or resisting soldier can stand in for all these experiences. The historian’s task is to distinguish them without treating hatred of one dictatorship as evidence of what the other would actually provide. Prisoners were already entering a system prepared to deny important protections. The Commissar Order prescribed the killing of a category of captured political personnel, while the May jurisdiction decree had weakened restraints on violence against civilians. Their existence does not establish the date or perpetrators of every local killing on 22 June. It does establish the policy environment into which prisoners and civilians were being delivered. The invasion’s social consequences cannot be postponed to a separate narrative beginning only after the armies had finished moving. [11] [12] The same chronological care is necessary when discussing Soviet violence. Prison massacres committed during the retreat would become central to the history of particular cities in the following days. They should be investigated through the institutions and personnel responsible, rather than used as a collective accusation against an ethnic group. German and local antisemitic propaganda would deliberately collapse those distinctions. The studies that follow will examine the documented killings and the exploitation of their discovery in their own settings, especially in western Ukraine. On the first day, the immediate fact was that military retreat was also dismantling institutions whose prisoners remained exposed to the decisions of their guards and superiors.

What the first day settled—and what it did not

In Britain, Churchill’s broadcast of 22 June placed opposition to Hitler ahead of his longstanding hostility to communism. He offered assistance to the Soviet Union while making no claim to have revised his judgment of its political system. This was an immediate strategic realignment, but not the instant creation of a fully functioning coalition supply system. The Soviet armies fighting that day were using the resources they already possessed. Assistance promised abroad could matter enormously over time; it could not restore a telephone line, replace a destroyed aircraft or bring fuel to an isolated tank formation that evening. [13] Washington’s public response followed on 23 June. Acting Secretary of State Sumner Welles condemned both dictatorships while identifying resistance to Hitler as serving American security. The distinction between the date of invasion and the date of this statement matters: it was a reaction to the first day, not a decision already shaping the Soviet battle on the morning of 22 June. Its practical implications would have to be worked out through diplomacy, production, shipping and Soviet willingness to disclose requirements. The invasion changed the possibilities of cooperation more quickly than it changed the material balance at the front. [14]

The evening snapshot

Read a spearhead as a spearhead

The German atlas labels this sheet as the evening situation on 22 June. Its forward symbols describe reported military positions and assessments. They do not prove that every road, village or forest behind the leading units was securely occupied. That distinction becomes particularly important as isolated Soviet resistance survives behind the moving front. [6]

Measured against the documented German purpose of breaking the frontier system and preventing an orderly Soviet withdrawal, the first day was an exceptionally powerful beginning. It opened opportunities for the encirclements to come and reduced the Soviet command’s ability to control events. Measured against the ultimate objective of destroying the Soviet capacity to wage war, it was evidence of initial effectiveness rather than a completed verdict. There was no reliable basis on 22 June for treating every tank, reserve formation or industrial resource beyond the frontier as already neutralized. [15] The day’s most useful lesson is therefore more precise than either a story of irresistible German progress or a catalogue of Soviet heroism. Germany had made its operation work across enough critical points to put entire Soviet armies in danger. Soviet soldiers had demonstrated that surprise did not eliminate resistance, but their resistance frequently lacked the organization needed to change the wider result. Between those two facts lay the battles of the next several days. On 25 June, the counterattacks around Raseiniai and in western Ukraine would test whether the Red Army could turn surviving strength into a coordinated interruption of the invasion.

sourceMethod: Numbered notes link to the source list and return to their first use. Page and document references accompany the relevant notes. German situation maps and staff reports are evidence of what German headquarters recorded, not an omniscient picture of the battlefield. Soviet operational records are cited from the General Staff’s published documentary collections, accessed in transcription; archival identifiers are those printed in those collections. Orders establish intentions; they do not by themselves prove execution. Postwar military accounts are checked against dated records and identified as retrospective. Place names follow familiar historical usage, with present-day equivalents where useful.
